title: Lesson 73: Enterprise Integration Patterns: Routers, Translators, Aggregators, and EIP
description: The shared vocabulary of enterprise integration: the Enterprise Integration Patterns (EIP) catalog, the Message Router that decides where a message goes without changing it, the Message Translator that adapts one format or contract to another, and the Aggregator that combines related messages into one result.

questions.question: An architect is routing one inbound Case to different assignment queues based on its priority, then plans to enrich the record with account data from a separate API call. Per the lesson's shapes, which two named patterns does this design use, and which property must the routing step respect?
options: A Message Router for the priority-based routing and a Content Enricher for the account lookup, with the router directed not to modify the message contents.
An Aggregator for the priority-based routing and a Content Filter for the account lookup, with the aggregator directed to modify the message contents.
A Content-Based Router combined with a Splitter, with the router allowed to reshape the message as it decides the destination.
A Resequencer for the routing and a Canonical Data Model for the enricher, with the enricher allowed to drop the priority field.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the Message Router as a filter that decides a message's destination without modifying the message contents, and the Content Enricher as the transformation that adds data a sender did not provide. The routing step must never also reshape the message, which is the router discipline the lesson emphasizes.

questions.question: An ERP requires XML while Salesforce uses JSON, and a review asks why the integration defines one internal canonical Customer contract instead of mapping each pair of systems directly. Which reasoning does the lesson give?
options: A canonical model converts N-times-M source-to-target mappings into N plus M, which is why it makes the translator family maintainable as more systems join.
A canonical model removes the need for any translators because every system adopts the same binary payload over the wire.
A canonical model only helps when there are exactly two systems, so it is the wrong choice for a many-system integration.
A canonical model is required by External Services and cannot be built in Apex.
questions.explanation: The lesson says translating every source to every target is N-times-M translations, while translating each source to one canonical model and each target from it is N plus M, and it calls the Canonical Data Model the translator family's organizing principle that keeps integrations maintainable as systems join.

questions.question: A quoting service fans a request out to three banks and must return the best rate, but speed matters more than waiting for every response. Which completeness condition does the lesson direct this design to use, and why?
options: First best, which waits for the first response and ignores the rest, practical in a bidding or quoting scenario where response time is critical.
Wait for all, which never publishes until every bank has answered, guaranteeing the best possible rate.
External event, which waits for the end of a trading day before combining any responses.
A fixed count of zero, so the aggregator publishes an empty combined result immediately.
questions.explanation: The lesson lists the aggregator completeness strategies and describes first best as waiting only for the first fastest response and ignoring the others, calling it practical in a bidding or quoting scenario where response time is critical, which matches the quote use case.
